course: If you are interested in magnetic materials, this is the best course you could take. The aim is to help students to gain a perspective on magnetic materials.

I think it is a must-take course for every material science student. I believe it is very important to have the most basic knowledge on such matters, especially due to the increasing number of spintronic applications nowadays. As the positive aspects, the coursework given to the students does not take excessive time and it is taken into account that each student also has their research. I think this is a big plus. It was also very logical to start from the very basics and go into the details later, and to do the numerical part at the beginning and then explain the applications. The only negative aspects I can say are the homework given consecutively during the first 6 weeks and the midterm. Maybe the number of questions in homework can be reduced because it is hard to find free-time to solve questions each week.

I liked the fact that it spanned the physics, the materials, and the applications. I didn't like the fact that it was fast with the physics, so I had difficulty following and was too detailed with some applications.

Usually, homework and open-ended tasks take more time than exams and quizzes and do not motivate the students to focus on the lectures, so perhaps make the coursework a little less open-ended and a little more connected with the specific material of the lectures. The advantage, of course, is that we can work on projects connected to our research, but this won't work for everyone.

course: The lecture includes physics of magnetic materials and their applications. Since the magnetic materials is highly popular, learning their fundamental properties and physical aspects was incredibly exciting.

Having enough time to complete assignments and the midterm is a significant advantage. While weekly quizzes and the project can be tiring a little bit, they can also be viewed positively, as they help reinforce knowledge and sustain student interest, I mean, it depends on the person. For me, it wasn’t an issue.

Extremely enlightening course; I suggest every grad student with engineering background should take it to gain very important intuition to not only magnetic properties, but about quantum mechanics and microstructures in general. It is a bonus that the instructor was incredibly meticulous on preliminary QM part, which was essential for students who has never seen these concepts before but I can imagine them being unnecessary/boring for students with physics background.

The coursework is okay and there are some extra resources like books on magnetism for students to work with, but the relevant literature on the subject is a bit complicated because authors of said books are not writing in a coherent way amongst themselves, which makes some explanations vary too much thus makes research and homeworks a little frustrating.

We had quizzes every week but I do not think it was a bad thing; it kept us stuck with the class and learned the topic very well. On the other hand, quizzes were not that hard. Also, from homework and project, you can learn a lot about new stuff.
Course covers the basics to advanced topics
